title: Fanatics Collect attempting to address card seller ‘pain point’ with new payout option
content:
Battles between auction houses and marketplaces for customers to consign valuable sports trading cards occur on a daily basis, with each company making sales pitches as to why someone would receive the most money in selling through them.

Fanatics Collect is attempting to up the ante for sellers by launching FanCash payouts for customers, which waives transaction fees from anywhere between six and 12 percent that typically accompanies any sale.

But there’s a catch — FanCash, Fanatics’ “loyalty currency,” can only be used within the company’s ecosystem: Fanatics Collect, Fanatics.com, Topps, online breaks, tickets and memorabilia.

The consignor would have to select the “FanCash payout” option before listing the item. It can be applied through a “buy now” or auction sale.

Fees charged by eBay, the largest marketplace in the sports collectibles space, stand at 13.25 percent on a total amount of the sale up to $7,500 calculated per item and another 2.35 percent on the portion of sales over $7,500. Many top auction houses charge fees that can top 20 percent. However, auction houses sometimes reduce or wave fees entirely on certain items they want to be attached to. The size of these fees often plays a role in where people decide to sell their collectibles.

Fanatics Collect CEO Nick Bell told The Athletic that this move is a component in the company’s efforts to alter its fee structure as it tries to address one of the aspects of the business that sellers commonly complain about.

“I think from a very early point in Fanatics Collect’s history we’ve been mapping and tracking the pain points for collectors,” Bell said. “And I think we’ve got now a pretty strategic and focused kind of approach to those pain points. Fees, I think, was an obvious one. At first pass, it’s like, well we’re a marketplace. It’s really hard to do anything about fees. OK, what can we do?  How can we reduce fees? How can we make our own service operation so that collectors keep more of the proceeds?

“Then, as FanCash started to grow within the business, it just seemed like an obvious opportunity. … We’re committed to it. This is something that we think long term is going to drive significant value for collectors, and hopefully it will turn casual collectors into long-term collectors.”

While eliminating fees may appear to be a costly experiment in the company’s efforts to increase its share of the collectibles marketplace landscape, anyone who chooses the FanCash payout option is committing the full sale price to be spent within the Fanatics ecosystem in a way that the company sees as a benefit to both itself and the seller.

“We obviously did the math, but I think it’s something that we can get comfortable with for the benefit that we think (FanCash) gets to collectors,” Bell said. “Yes, it’s a cost for the business, but we think it’s a cost that’s worthwhile with the overall drive to service collectors.”

Cash payouts for items sold on Fanatics Collect will maintain transaction fees.

“I think if you look at our fee structure, it’s already one of the most competitive in the market,” Bell said. “I think from our point of view, what we’re really focused on is collectors building their collections.”

Trading cards have become an increasingly lucrative category for online marketplaces as the collectibles industry has boomed in recent years. According to Card Ladder, which tracks online sales across different marketplaces, eBay had trading card sales of  $487.89 million in June, while Fanatics was its closest competitor at $83.35 million.
